lens: A, true on this machine, Linux half (Ubuntu 24.04, kernel 7.0, systemd 255, cgroup v2, psutil 7.2.2; run as the signed-in user, never as root)

findings.title: Tagging a run the usual systemd way switches on the cpu controller and changes how the CPU is shared among the user's apps
findings.evidence: uv run python docs/review/probes/a-linux/cgroup_side_effects.py (out.txt): 'app.slice passes down, before: memory pids' / 'Delegate=yes: scope has [cpu memory pids]; app.slice passes down [cpu memory pids] while it runs; ... cpu.weight True' / 'Delegate=memory pids: scope has [memory pids]; app.slice passes down [memory pids] while it runs; cpu.stat True, memory.peak True, cpu.weight False' / 'cgroups directly below app.slice that the change applies to: 22'. Part 2, one busy process in X against four in Y on one CPU, no weight written: 'cpu controller not passed down to X and Y: X gets 20%' / 'passed down: X gets 50%'. Kernel doc https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/cgroup-v2.html on cpu.stat: 'This file exists whether the controller is enabled or not.' docs/17-build-prompt.md:23 and :69 forbid limits but say nothing about controllers.
findings.impact: While any tagged run is live, the 22 app groups next to it change from per-thread to per-group CPU sharing. A tagged 'pytest -n 8' then gets half the CPU against one busy browser instead of 8/9. That changes the scheduling of processes Submeter did not launch, which breaks fixed rule 1, and it changes the CPU figures Submeter is measuring. It also enables cpu.weight, which is the setting a priority change would use.
findings.proposed_change: docs/17-build-prompt.md, after 'Set no limits on the group' (line 69): 'On Linux, delegate only the memory and pids controllers (Delegate="memory pids"). Never enable the cpu or io controller and never write cpu.weight: switching cpu on changes CPU sharing for every sibling group, and cpu.stat is present without it.' docs/09-telemetry.md row 1, Linux column: 'cgroup v2 with memory and pids delegated; cpu.stat is always present'.
findings.refutation_attempt: I checked whether cpu was already passed down in app.slice. It was not: 'memory pids', confirmed again by cat of app.slice/cgroup.subtree_control. I checked whether the design needs the cpu controller at all. It does not: cpu.stat is present under Delegate=memory pids and in a group with no controllers (cgroup_totals A: 'cpu.stat yes'). I checked whether the change stays after the run: it reverts ('afterwards: memory pids'), so the effect lasts only while a tagged run is live. The 20% and 50% shares match per-thread and per-group fairness exactly, so load from the other reviewers did not decide the result.

findings.title: The brief never says where a Linux tagged cgroup can live; the only place that works unprivileged is a delegated systemd user scope with holder and payload leaf groups
findings.evidence: cgroup_scope.out.txt: user.slice and user-N.slice are owned by root; user@N.service is the only subtree this user owns ('Delegate=pids memory cpu'); this shell's vte-spawn scope has 'Delegate=no' and 'passes down nothing'. cgroup_totals.out.txt A: a group made below the shell's own cgroup has 'cpu.stat yes, memory.current NO, memory.peak NO, pids.current NO'. B (directly below user@N.service): everything except io. cgroup_scope 2-3: a transient scope with Delegate gets controllers, but 'passing memory down while this process is in it: refused (Device or resource busy)', 'moving this process into a sub-group: allowed', payload CPU 'kernel 0.646515' vs 'wait4 0.646941', memory.peak readable after its last process ended. Once the scope empties, the 'scope directory, with the sub-groups made inside it, still there: False' and systemctl reports 'LoadState=not-found'. cgroup_totals 2: a mkdir group is 'still there: True; populated 0' two seconds after its last process exited. cgroup_scope 4: with no session bus, 'Failed to connect to bus: No medium found'. cgroup_leaving 1: a move whose common ancestor has a root-owned cgroup.procs is 'refused (Permission denied)'. Quotes: https://systemd.io/CGROUP_DELEGATION/ 'Never create your own cgroups below arbitrary cgroups systemd manages, i.e cgroups you haven't set Delegate= in.' https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/cgroup-v2.html 'Non-root cgroups can distribute domain resources to their children only when they don't have any processes of their own.' and 'The writer must have write access to the "cgroup.procs" file of the common ancestor of the source and destination cgroups.'
findings.impact: The phase 2 gate depends on choices the brief leaves to guesswork. A group made with mkdir under the shell's scope gives CPU time only and breaks systemd's single-writer rule. A group under user@UID.service works but also breaks that rule. A plain systemd scope is deleted the moment it empties, so its final totals are lost unless a holder process lives inside it. Groups made with mkdir are never removed by the kernel, so every crashed run leaks a directory. R15's wording 'a cgroup is removed once it is empty' is true only for systemd scopes. su, sudo -u, cron and WSL without systemd have no user bus, so tagged runs cannot work there.
findings.proposed_change: docs/17-build-prompt.md, a Linux paragraph after line 62: 'On Linux, ask the signed-in user's systemd over the user bus for a transient scope with Delegate="memory pids", as systemd-run --user --scope does. Inside it make two leaf groups: payload for the command and holder for the waiting process, because a group that passes controllers down may hold no processes. The holder watches payload/cgroup.events. When populated is 0 it reads cpu.stat, memory.peak, memory.stat and pids.peak, writes the run file and exits, and systemd then removes the scope. Never make cgroups outside such a scope. Without a user bus (su, sudo -u, cron, a system service, WSL without systemd), say that tagged runs are unavailable and run the command polled.' docs/16-review-log.md R15: 'systemd removes a scope once it is empty; a cgroup made with mkdir stays until it is removed'.
findings.cost: One paragraph in docs/17 and one corrected clause in R15.
findings.refutation_attempt: I searched docs/ for cgroup, systemd and delegat. The only Linux guidance is docs/09:9 ('memory and io files where delegated') and docs/17:42 ('check current documentation'). Neither names the scope, the sub-group layout or what happens with no user bus. R15 covers the vanishing totals, not where the group lives. I confirmed delegation with 'systemctl show user@UID.service' ('DelegateControllers=cpu memory pids'). I confirmed that no probe cgroup remains: find /sys/fs/cgroup -name 'submeter-probe*' gives 0.

findings.title: On Linux a tagged group has no kernel I/O totals and no count of processes started, though docs/17 calls both authoritative
findings.evidence: cgroup_whole_machine.out.txt: delegated to this user, 74 cgroups, 'io.stat present in 0'; elsewhere 'io.stat present in 158'. cgroup_totals B: 'passing io: refused (No such file or directory)'. /usr/lib/systemd/system/user@.service line 24: 'Delegate=pids memory cpu'. cgroup_totals 2: 'files that count processes ever started: none' (it lists every file in the group). cgroup_totals 3: 'one process with 8 extra threads: pids.current 9, lines in cgroup.procs 1'. Kernel doc https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/cgroup-v2.html: 'Note that PIDs used in this controller refer to TIDs, process IDs as used by the kernel.' Claims: docs/17-build-prompt.md:62 'The kernel's totals for the group are authoritative: CPU time, memory, I/O and process counts, including processes that have already exited'; docs/05-data-flow.md:52 'the kernel totals CPU, memory and I/O for every process in a tagged group'; docs/09-telemetry.md:9 'Without admin: Full'; docs/17:127 run totals include 'I/O, processes started'.
findings.impact: Run totals for 'I/O' and 'processes started' have no kernel source on Linux. Enabling io delegation needs a system drop-in, which breaks fixed rule 2. A builder who takes pids.peak as 'processes' reports threads. A builder who reports I/O as zero or polls it silently undercounts, which breaks priority 1 ('never show a wrong number').
findings.proposed_change: docs/09-telemetry.md row 1: Linux 'cpu.stat, memory.* and pids.* (tasks, not processes); no io.stat without root', Without admin 'Partial'. docs/17-build-prompt.md:62: add 'On Linux the kernel gives CPU time and memory only. Processes started is the number seen, shown as a lower bound. I/O comes from the source chosen below, or is shown as unavailable.' docs/05-data-flow.md:52: 'CPU and memory (and I/O on Windows)'.
findings.cost: Three sentences across three documents, plus the owner's choice below.
findings.decision_question: Where should tagged-run I/O come from on Linux? (a) The launcher reads its own /proc/self/io after waiting for the command. The kernel folds reaped children's I/O into the reaper (io_children 2: '+32.0 MB' through an intermediate shell). This is complete for every descendant reaped inside the tree, misses double-forked orphans, and changes no process. (b) Option (a), with the holder also set as a child subreaper (PR_SET_CHILD_SUBREAPER) so orphans come back to it. This is complete, but it changes which process adopts the tree's orphans. (c) Show tagged I/O as unavailable on Linux. Recommendation: (a) now, with doctor stating the orphan gap. (b) only if you judge that subreaping is not a change to a process; I did not probe it.
findings.refutation_attempt: I looked for a user-writable way to get io: the only route is a root drop-in for user@.service. I looked for a started-process counter among all 50 files in a group (listed in cgroup_totals 2): pids.events counts only hits on the limit. The docs/09 hedge 'where delegated' does not save the claim, because the row still says 'Full' and docs/17:62 and docs/05:52 state I/O without the hedge.

findings.title: On Linux a parent's /proc/PID/io includes the I/O of children it has reaped, so the polled path double-counts I/O
findings.evidence: uv run python docs/review/probes/a-linux/io_children.py, run through the baseline PsutilProvider and Sampler (io_children.py:22-24,59-82): 'child while alive, after writing: write_bytes +32.0 MB' / 'this probe before reaping the child: +0.0 MB' / 'after reaping the child: write_bytes +32.0 MB' / 'interval in which the child wrote: child 32.0 MB, probe 0.0 MB' / 'interval in which it was reaped: probe 32.0 MB (child gone)' / 'a workload holding both is charged 64.0 MB for 32 MB written'. Through a shell that only waits: '+32.0 MB' after reaping the shell. The sampler takes a plain per-key delta (src/submeter/collector/sampler.py:80-83), and aggregate sums it (src/submeter/attribution/rules.py:208-209).
findings.impact: Any polled workload whose children are seen alive gets their I/O twice, once from the child and again in the parent's jump at reap time. Grandchildren are folded in through each reaper. Workload io_bytes_per_s, I/O run totals and the I/O-bound evidence are inflated by up to 2x, or more for deep trees. docs/09:12 presents /proc/<pid>/io as a plain per-process counter.
findings.proposed_change: docs/09-telemetry.md row 'Disk I/O per process', Linux: '/proc/<pid>/io, which also includes children the process has reaped'. docs/17-build-prompt.md:71: 'On Linux, /proc/PID/io and the child-time counters both absorb reaped children. When a child that was seen ends, subtract its last-seen counters from its reaper's next increase. Short-lived children that were never seen are recovered by this, not lost.' Add a test with this probe's shape to the phase-1 /proc reader.
findings.cost: Two sentences of brief; the subtraction is about 30 lines in the phase-1 /proc reader and sampler.
findings.refutation_attempt: I checked whether psutil's io_counters reads something other than /proc/PID/io: it does not (the _pslinux io_counters path). I checked whether the probe double-counted by its own design: the two deltas come from the unmodified baseline sampler at three snapshots. I searched docs/ and R01-R37 for reap, children and io: there is no mention. The Windows per-process counters are not involved; this is Linux only.

findings.title: 'Recover reaped children's CPU time from the parent's child-time counters' overcounts by 50% as written; it is exact only with a subtraction rule and has hard limits
findings.evidence: child_times.out.txt part 2, 80 children polled every 0.5 s: 'truth, from wait4 inside the parent: 13.23 s' / 'polling alone ... 6.63 s' / 'polling plus the parent's counter: 19.85 s (+50%)' / 'the same, less the last sighting of each child that ended: 13.22 s'. child_times_tree.out.txt, a parent, a child and 12 grandchildren: 'truth 6.15 s' / 'polling plus every counter: 14.56 s' / 'less the last own time of each process that ended: 9.36 s' / 'less the last counter of each process that ended as well: 6.15 s'. Limits from child_times part 1: an orphaned grandchild gives 'parent's counter shows 0.00 s; adopted by systemd ... whose own counter rose by 1.02 s'; with SIGCHLD ignored, '0.00 s'. Counters on this machine: 'this user's service manager ... reaped children 11,138 s'; largest counter 'claude 87,945 s'. Brief: docs/17-build-prompt.md:71 (one sentence), docs/05-data-flow.md:65; docs/10-known-limits.md:10 states the limit for Windows only.
findings.impact: A builder who follows the sentence literally adds cutime and cstime deltas to what polling saw and inflates spawn-heavy polled workloads by 50% or more. When a long-lived process ends, its whole counter jumps into its parent: a terminal shell's workload would be charged 24 h of CPU in one interval when the claude process inside it exits. Orphans, auto-reaped children and children whose parent outlives the window are never recovered, and nothing says so.
findings.proposed_change: docs/17-build-prompt.md:71: replace the sentence with 'On Linux, add each process's increase in child time (cutime + cstime). When a process that was seen ends, subtract its last-seen own CPU time and its last-seen child time from its reaper's next increase. This recovers the CPU time of descendants reaped inside the tree. It cannot recover orphans adopted by the user's service manager, children of a parent that ignores SIGCHLD, or children not yet reaped.' docs/10-known-limits.md:10: add the Linux case with those three gaps.
findings.cost: Three sentences in docs/17 and one table cell in docs/10.
findings.refutation_attempt: I tried the obvious correction (subtract last sightings), and it is exact for one level (13.22 vs 13.23) and, with the counter subtracted as well, for trees (6.15 vs 6.15). So the method works and the defect is that the brief leaves the rule out. R01 covers the polling gap, not this recovery step.

findings.title: Linux can place CPU time that polling missed, per systemd unit, from cgroup cpu.stat, which every cgroup exposes to an unprivileged user; the brief does not use it
findings.evidence: cgroup_whole_machine.out.txt: '235 cgroups'; cpu.stat 'present in 74, readable in 74' (delegated) and 'present in 161, readable in 161' (elsewhere). 8 s with one spawner of 78 short children: 'machine busy, /proc/stat: 12.86 CPU-s' / 'root cgroup cpu.stat: 12.85' / 'sum of cpu.stat over the top-level cgroups: 12.81 (every task, exited or not)' / 'every process polled from /proc at 1 s: 5.18 (40% of that)' / 'cpu.stat of the cgroup that held the spawner, whole run: 6.54; its children, from wait4: 6.48'. Lead's measure/reconcile_under_spawn.out.txt: with four spawners, 'missing 71.28 CPU-s = 51.6% of capacity'.
findings.impact: The 2% reconciliation invariant (docs/17:98) fails by 14 to 52% of capacity under spawn loads on Linux, and nothing says where the missing time goes. If it is put in System, the System bucket stops meaning 'kernel and interrupts', which here are 0.10 of 12.86 CPU-s. Per-cgroup cpu.stat closes the gap without root and names the unit (terminal scope, browser scope, service) where the unseen processes ran.
findings.proposed_change: docs/17-build-prompt.md, Reconciliation invariant (line 98): 'On Linux, read cpu.stat of every leaf cgroup each tick. For each cgroup, the increase minus the sum of the polled process deltas inside it is CPU time of processes polling missed. Show it as "unseen processes in <unit>" under the workload that owns that cgroup's processes, or under Unattributed, never under System.' This becomes a phase-1 task for providers.process on Linux.
findings.cost: One paragraph of brief; one provider task (roughly 235 small file reads a tick on this machine, not timed here).
findings.refutation_attempt: I checked that the user can read cpu.stat outside its delegated subtree: 161 of 161 readable. I checked that top-level cpu.stat adds up to the machine's busy time: 12.81 of 12.86. I checked that a scope's cpu.stat matches its children's wait4 sum (6.54 vs 6.48, the spawner itself making the difference). It overlaps the lead's reconciliation lead 1, but the Linux remedy is new.

findings.title: A tagged group's kernel memory figure includes page cache, so on Linux it is a different unit from the PSS used for every other workload
findings.evidence: cgroup_totals.out.txt part 5, a child writes a 64 MB file and exits: 'the child's own peak resident memory: 16.6 MB' / 'memory.current before 1.0 MB, after 66.3 MB, memory.peak 70.2 MB, populated 0' / 'memory.stat: anon 0.0 MB, file 64.0 MB'. smaps_cost.out.txt part 3: vte-spawn scope 'PSS 1.88' vs 'memory.current 2.34, memory.peak 3.76 ... anon 1.69, file 0.44'; firefox scope 'PSS 1.41' vs '1.75 ... file 0.50'; thunderbird scope 'PSS 0.47' vs '0.88 ... file 0.60' (GB). The brief says workload totals use USS or PSS (docs/17-build-prompt.md:81; docs/06-storage.md:83) and gives no unit for tagged groups.
findings.impact: A tagged build that writes artifacts reports a peak memory near its I/O volume (70 MB for a 17 MB process), and the memory stays charged to an empty group. Tagged and polled workloads are compared in different units, which here differ by 24 to 87%. Run-over-run diffs of peak memory (docs/17:127) track file writes, not memory.
findings.proposed_change: docs/17-build-prompt.md, Memory paragraph (line 81): 'For a tagged group on Linux, the comparable figure is memory.stat anon plus memory.swap.current. memory.current and memory.peak include page cache; store the peak labelled as such and never add it to PSS.' docs/06-storage.md:83: note the Linux tagged unit.
findings.refutation_attempt: I checked whether the brief already names a kernel memory field for groups: it does not (docs/09:9 says only 'memory ... files'). I checked that the excess is page cache and not a process: memory.stat attributes it to 'file' with 'populated 0'. Whether the Windows Job peak is committed memory, which would make the two platforms disagree, I did not verify; it needs Microsoft documentation.

findings.title: The built-in 'memory nearly full' alert and the commit tile read 264-274% on a normal Linux desktop and would stay at serious
findings.evidence: linux_sources.out.txt: 'Committed_AS / CommitLimit = 2.74 with vm.overcommit_memory = 0; memory in use = 0.69 of RAM'. Rechecked from /proc/meminfo: CommitLimit 12064156 kB, Committed_AS 31893448 kB (2.64), overcommit_memory 0. Kernel doc https://docs.kernel.org/filesystems/proc.html on CommitLimit: 'This limit is only adhered to if strict overcommit accounting is enabled (mode 2 in 'vm.overcommit_memory').' Brief: docs/08-configuration.md:138 'commit_fraction | machine | Memory commit as a share of the commit limit' and :148 'memory nearly full | machine | commit_fraction | above 0.90 | 2m | serious' (switched on by default); docs/02-what-it-looks-like.md:31 'Memory commit' tile; docs/13-build-list.md:16 providers.system collects commit.
findings.impact: On Linux under the default heuristic overcommit, the default serious alert fires two minutes after start and never clears, and the commit tile shows over 100%. The live diagnosis job is noisy from the first minute. The Linux verdict column (docs/07:98) correctly uses PSI, so only the alert and the tile are wrong.
findings.proposed_change: docs/08-configuration.md:138: 'commit_fraction: Windows; on Linux only when vm.overcommit_memory = 2, otherwise unavailable'. :148: on Linux the built-in rule uses memory pressure (PSI memory full) or available memory instead. docs/02-what-it-looks-like.md:31: the Linux tile shows available memory.
findings.refutation_attempt: I checked whether the brief already splits commit by platform: docs/07:98 does for the verdict, but docs/08's metric list and built-in alert do not, and docs/09:20 lists commit only under Windows pressure signals, which a builder could read either way. I rechecked the ratio on a second read: 2.64.

findings.title: On Linux, process identity and the 'born this interval' test use a wall-clock start time; psutil itself uses the boot-relative start time because the wall one moves
findings.evidence: Code: .venv/lib/python3.14/site-packages/psutil/_pslinux.py:1849-1863 ('starttime ... is unaffected by system clock updates' ... 'Add the boot time ... This is subject to system clock updates'). psutil/__init__.py:390-394: on Linux, psutil's own identity uses create_time(monotonic=True) 'since it is stable over changes to system time'. __init__.py:2383-2388, boot_time 'may be affected by changes such as manual adjustments or time synchronization (e.g. NTP)'. The baseline uses the wall form (src/submeter/providers/psutil_provider.py:57) and compares it with wall time (sampler.py:84). process_identity.out.txt 2: 'btime equals floor(wall clock - time since boot): True'; 'a step forward of 0.075 s or back of 0.925 s moves btime ... by a whole second'. Part 3, simulated by replacing psutil's boot_time and time.time: 'interval with the step: child's start minus its parent's -3597 s, workload 'unattributed' ... CPU credited 0.00 s of 0.46 s', and 'a later interval: ... 'unattributed''. Part 4, a provider that recomputes the start time each tick with btime one second lower: '452 processes, 452 counted as started, 446 as exited, 0.15 CPU-s credited of 1.95 busy'. Suspend: man7 clock_gettime(2): CLOCK_MONOTONIC 'does not count time that the system is suspended'; CLOCK_BOOTTIME 'is identical to CLOCK_MONOTONIC, except that it also includes any time that the system is suspended'. The sampler detects suspend by wall minus monotonic (sampler.py:55).
findings.impact: After a backward wall-clock step (an NTP step, or a manual or dual-boot clock change), every child of an already-cached parent appears older than its parent. The parent link is then rejected (rules.py:146) and the child stays unattributed until the parent restarts, and its first interval's CPU is dropped. A /proc reader that adds btime each tick re-keys all processes whenever btime shifts by a second: about 450 false starts and exits, process-table churn (R25), and one interval of lost CPU. A forward step over 2 s is recorded as a suspend gap.
findings.proposed_change: docs/17-build-prompt.md:77: 'On Linux the start time in the identity is field 22 of /proc/PID/stat, an integer count of ticks since boot, paired with /proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id. Convert it to wall time only for display. Compare start times, and test whether a process was born in an interval, on the boot clock. Detect suspend as the growth of CLOCK_BOOTTIME minus CLOCK_MONOTONIC.' Baseline: ProcessKey.started on Linux becomes boot-relative (psutil_provider.py:57), and Snapshot carries a boot-clock time for sampler.py:84.
findings.cost: Two sentences of brief and about 30 lines across psutil_provider.py, models.py and sampler.py.
findings.refutation_attempt: I tested whether keys differ between processes without a step: no, 448 of 448 are identical between two Python processes, and identical with /proc field 22 + btime in both float orders. So the defect needs a clock step, and I did not step the real clock (that needs root). The step was simulated by replacing the two functions that read the clock. That btime follows the wall clock rests on the floor(wall - boottime) check and psutil's own docstrings. The severity stays medium because large backward steps are uncommon.

findings.title: On Linux the command lines of other users' processes are readable, and the baseline reads and keeps them, against the brief's privacy statement
findings.evidence: proc_readability.out.txt: /proc mount options 'rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec,relatime' (no hidepid). 'other user: stat readable 134, statm 134, status 134, cmdline 134; io, smaps_rollup, cwd, exe, fd denied 134'. 'other users' processes whose command line shows arguments: 67'. 'baseline provider ... restricted with command line read: 299'. ground/platform-check.txt: '452 processes, 298 restricted, 0 without a readable command line'. Code: psutil_provider.py:67-71 reads cmdline for every process. Brief: docs/10-known-limits.md:16 'Command lines and USS are not readable'; docs/02-what-it-looks-like.md:150-153 '14 processes owned by other users ... Command lines and USS are not readable, because Submeter never runs elevated.' Kernel doc https://docs.kernel.org/filesystems/proc.html: 'hidepid=invisible or hidepid=2 means hidepid=1 plus all /proc/<pid>/ will be fully invisible to other users.'
findings.impact: On a shared Linux machine, Submeter would store other people's and root's command-line arguments (redacted only for secrets) in its raw files, which contradicts the stated behaviour. Nothing leaves the machine, so fixed rule 3 holds, but the privacy statement is false. With hidepid=2, the opposite happens: other users' processes are absent from /proc and drop out of Restricted entirely, which the brief also does not cover.
findings.proposed_change: docs/10-known-limits.md:16 and docs/02-what-it-looks-like.md:150-153, Linux wording: 'CPU time, memory, names and command lines are readable; I/O, USS, working folder and executable path are not. Submeter keeps only the name of another user's process.' Provider (psutil_provider.py:68 and the phase-1 /proc reader): leave cmdline as None when the process's uid differs from the collector's. doctor reports hidepid from the /proc mount options.
findings.cost: Two text cells and about five lines of provider code.
findings.refutation_attempt: I checked whether redaction (R04) answers this: it removes secrets, not other users' arguments in general, and the brief promises those are unreadable. I checked ptrace_scope (1): it does not protect cmdline. Counts only; no command line was saved.

findings.title: On Linux the Restricted bucket would hold two-thirds of all processes, including every kernel thread, because the baseline marks a process restricted when only its I/O is unreadable
findings.evidence: proc_readability.out.txt: 'baseline provider: 452 processes, 299 restricted'; 'restricted by owner: other user 134, kernel thread 162, own user 3'; 'with no rules, workloads are: restricted 299, unattributed 153'. restricted_split.out.txt (new): 'own user 156 ... 54.3%', 'other user 133, io denied 133, 70,416 s, 42.2%', 'kernel thread 158, io denied 158, 5,907 s, 3.5%', and 'kernel threads found by PF_KTHREAD: 158'. Code: psutil_provider.py:79-80 sets restricted on an io AccessDenied. Brief: docs/17-build-prompt.md:97 'System (kernel, interrupts)'; the mock shows 'Restricted 14 processes' (docs/03-cli-output.md:63).
findings.impact: Kernel threads (kworker, ksoftirqd, kswapd), which the brief means to put in System, land in Restricted. Restricted then means 'I/O unknown', not 'unreadable', and holds about 46% of CPU time since start on this machine, although that CPU time is fully known. The CPU numbers stay correct; the labels mislead.
findings.proposed_change: docs/17-build-prompt.md:97: 'On Linux, kernel threads (PF_KTHREAD in field 9 of /proc/PID/stat) count as System.' docs/10-known-limits.md:16: on Linux, Restricted means I/O and USS are missing. The provider's capability note says which fields are missing rather than 'not fully readable'.
findings.refutation_attempt: I checked whether rules still reach restricted processes: they do (rules.py:156 falls back to Restricted only when no rule matched). So naming works, and the impact is limited to the labels and to the kernel threads. The kernel-thread CPU share is small here (3.5%), which is why this is low.

findings.title: On Linux, rules match 'exe' against psutil's name(), which is often not the executable's file name, and the sample rules match almost nothing
findings.evidence: process_names.out.txt: '452 processes; the kernel's comm is 15 characters long for 109 of them'; 'psutil's name() is longer than comm, repaired from the command line: 61'; '20 set by the program itself or by its launcher', for example 'Isolated Web Co' is 'firefox', 'RDD Process' is 'thunderbird-bin'; '5 a script's name, the executable is an interpreter', for example 'apport-gtk' is 'python3.12'. One script started three ways gives 'submeter-probe-' / 'python3' / 'python3.14'. examples/rules.toml as shipped: '{restricted: 295, unattributed: 136, agent:untagged: 20}', so only 'claude' matches. Code: psutil_provider.py:92 'exe=process.name()'; rules.py:78 exact, lowercased set membership. docs/08-configuration.md:217-251 calls the field the executable and uses .exe names only.
findings.impact: Rules written by executable name silently miss truncated, retitled and interpreter-run processes on Linux, so attribution falls to Unattributed. A 'python' rule matches neither 'python3' nor 'python3.14'. The per-hour top executables (docs/17:128) are keyed by these unstable names: name() is not cached on POSIX and can change during a process's life.
findings.proposed_change: docs/08-configuration.md rules section: 'exe matches the executable's file name (on Linux from /proc/PID/exe for own processes, else the first word of the command line, else comm). name matches the process name. Both accept glob patterns, for example python3*.' Provider: store both. examples/rules.toml: add Linux names (firefox, chrome, code, python3*) or a note that the examples are Windows names.
findings.cost: A paragraph in docs/08, a field in the model and two lines in rules.py.
findings.refutation_attempt: I checked whether psutil's cmdline repair removes the problem: it fixes 61 truncations, not program-set titles or interpreter runs. With Linux names substituted, the browser rule claims 31 processes, so the rule mechanism works once the names are right. I checked whether include_children rescues Firefox's child processes: mostly yes ('crashhelper' is missed), but only when the parent matched by name.

findings.title: Linux cannot stop a tagged tree from leaving its group, and a nested 'submeter run' that asks systemd for a new scope removes its tree from the outer run
findings.evidence: cgroup_leaving.out.txt 2, commands started inside a tagged group: 'a plain child: still inside the group'; 'through systemd-run --user --scope: OUTSIDE the group: .../run-...scope'; 'through the launcher of a snap (firefox): OUTSIDE the group: .../snap.firefox.firefox-N.scope'. cgroup_totals 7: 'a tagged process moving itself to a sibling group: ended up in 'away'; CPU charged to the group it left: 0.002 s'; 'a group that holds a process passing memory to its children: refused (Device or resource busy)'. cgroup_totals 6: a nested group's usage counts in its parent and stays after removal ('inner used 0.578 s; B/run grew by 0.578 s'). cgroup_totals A: a sub-group of a group that passes nothing down has cpu.stat only. Brief: docs/17-build-prompt.md:62 'nested jobs' (Windows only) and :69 'Do not allow breakaway'.
findings.impact: 'Do not allow breakaway' has no Linux equivalent. Descendants launched through systemd-run, snap or flatpak launchers, or D-Bus activation run elsewhere, and the 'exact' kernel total silently omits them. An agent tagged with submeter run that runs 'submeter run --as builds -- pytest' would, under a new-scope design, take the build out of the agent's total.
findings.proposed_change: docs/17-build-prompt.md:69, Linux sentence: 'Linux cannot forbid leaving the group; polling still attributes such a process through its parent. A launcher that is already in a tagged group nests by making a sub-group of its own payload group. That inner group has CPU time only, because controllers cannot be passed down below a group that holds processes.' docs/10-known-limits.md: add a row for descendants started through systemd-run, snap or flatpak launchers, or D-Bus activation.
findings.cost: Two sentences and one table row.
findings.refutation_attempt: I checked whether polling recovers the escaped processes: yes when ppid still points into the tree (systemd-run --scope execs in place), which is why this is medium and not high. I checked whether this is R21: R21 covers work done by other, already-running processes, not the run's own descendants.

findings.title: On Linux, per-process GPU load is not 'NVML or AMD sysfs, Full': AMD sysfs is device-wide, Intel is missing, and the generic per-process source is own-user only
findings.evidence: linux_sources.out.txt: 'GPU: cards card1 i915, card2-5 evdi; NVML library None; AMD sysfs load files 0'; 'DRM fdinfo: 12 processes of this user hold a GPU client, fields [... drm-engine-render, drm-engine-video, drm-total-system0 ...]; 298 processes could not be inspected'. https://docs.kernel.org/gpu/amdgpu/thermal.html: 'The amdgpu driver provides a sysfs API for reading how busy the GPU is as a percentage.' and 'The SMU firmware computes a percentage of load based on the aggregate activity level in the IP cores.' (device-level). https://docs.kernel.org/gpu/drm-usage-stats.html: 'One purpose of this output is to enable writing as generic as practically feasible top(1) like userspace monitoring tools.' Brief: docs/09-telemetry.md:13 'NVML for NVIDIA, sysfs for AMD | Full'; docs/07-analysis.md:99 Linux GPU-bound 'NVML utilisation above 90%'.
findings.impact: On Intel and AMD Linux machines, a builder following docs/09 delivers no per-process GPU data and no GPU verdict, while doctor would claim 'Full'. Other users' GPU clients are invisible in any case.
findings.proposed_change: docs/09-telemetry.md:13, Linux: 'NVML for NVIDIA; DRM fdinfo (drm-engine-*) per process for i915, xe, amdgpu and others; amdgpu sysfs gpu_busy_percent for device load', Without admin 'Own user only'. docs/07-analysis.md:99: 'busiest DRM engine or NVML utilisation above 90%'.
findings.refutation_attempt: I looked for a per-process AMD file in the amdgpu sysfs documentation: the page mentions none. I could not test NVML (no NVIDIA card), so the NVML part of the row stands unverified.

findings.title: The default PSS/USS reading costs about 0.8% of a core on Linux, most of the 1% idle budget
findings.evidence: smaps_cost.out.txt, CPU time charged to the reader: 'resident 0.84 GB: smaps_rollup 24,570 us (29.3 ms per GB), status 18 us'; 'smaps_rollup for the 25 largest: 241.6 ms a round, which at one round every 30 s is 0.805% of a core'; 'for all 156: 326.0 ms'; 'the 25 largest hold 87% of the proportional memory'. Defaults: docs/08-configuration.md:66-67 uss_interval 30s, uss_top_n 25. Budget: R02 '1% at idle and 3% when active'.
findings.impact: With the defaults, the slow memory reading alone uses about 80% of the idle budget on a machine with 11 GB resident in the user's processes. The cost grows with resident size (about 25-30 ms of CPU per GB), so on a 32 GB machine it would exceed the budget before any polling runs.
findings.proposed_change: docs/08-configuration.md:66-67: state that the reading costs about 30 ms of CPU per GB resident on Linux, and that the overhead guard stretches uss_interval or shrinks uss_top_n first. docs/17-build-prompt.md:81: for tagged groups on Linux, take memory from memory.stat rather than smaps.
findings.refutation_attempt: The figure is process CPU time, not wall time, so other reviewers' load matters less, but it was measured at 02:52 while they may have been running and was not repeated. The 87% coverage of the top 25 confirms the top-N idea, so only the budget arithmetic is at issue.

findings.title: A pid reused while psutil's cache holds the old process is missing from two snapshots in the baseline, then counted with zero CPU
findings.evidence: process_identity.out.txt 5, a reused pid imitated by ageing psutil's cached object: 'snapshot 1: the process is missing from the snapshot' / 'snapshot 2: the process is missing' / 'snapshot 3: present ... first seen True, CPU credited 0.00 s' / 'credited 0.00 s in three intervals; it used 2.28 s'. Code: psutil/__init__.py:639-642 (is_running marks the pid reused and raises NoSuchProcess, which psutil_provider.py:102-103 turns into None); __init__.py:1540-1553 (process_iter removes the reused pid after computing new_pids, so it is skipped once more). /proc/sys/kernel/pid_max = 4194304.
findings.impact: This breaks 'never dropped' for the psutil fallback: the new process is in no bucket for two ticks and loses its first seconds of CPU. It is rare on Linux with pid_max at 4 M; on Windows, where psutil is the required fallback (R17), pids are reused faster (not verified here).
findings.proposed_change: src/submeter/providers/psutil_provider.py: when a pid that psutil.pids() lists raises NoSuchProcess, read it again through a fresh psutil.Process(pid) in the same tick; add a test that ages the cached object as this probe does.
findings.refutation_attempt: The reuse is imitated, not produced, which is how psutil's own tests imitate it; the code path is real psutil 7.2.2. On Linux the /proc reader replaces psutil, so the risk sits mainly with the Windows fallback, hence low.

nothing_found: Kernel CPU accounting for a tagged group is exact here: 200 sub-second children, cpu.stat 10.677 s against a wait4 sum of 10.678 s (-0.01%); a Delegate scope's payload 0.6465 s against 0.6469 s.
A mkdir group's totals (cpu.stat, memory.peak, pids.peak) stay readable after its last process exits; the directory remains until rmdir.
A background process left by the command stays in the group (its parent becomes the user's systemd), and the group cannot be removed while populated (EBUSY).
Nested groups are hierarchical: an inner group's CPU counts in its parent and stays there after the inner group is removed.
systemd-run --user --scope passes the command's exit code through (7).
ProcessKey is identical between two Python processes (448 of 448, bit for bit) and against /proc field 22 + btime in both float orders, as long as the clock is not stepped.

These docs/09 Linux rows hold as stated: CPU from /proc/PID/stat (readable for every process); PSS/USS from smaps_rollup own-user only; /proc/PID/io own-user only; hwmon temperatures (4 chips); cpufreq plus thermal_throttle counters (8 of 8 CPUs, Intel); battery; RAPL root-only (mode 0o400, owner uid 0); connections own-user only (system-wide socket list readable, 32 of 90 with no visible process).
PSI cpu, memory and io are readable system-wide and per cgroup. The system 'full' line for CPU is present but zero, and the design's Linux CPU verdict uses 'some', which is correct.
The Linux bottleneck verdict's memory signal (PSI memory full, docs/07:98) is sound; the commit problem is limited to the commit_fraction alert and tile.
No probe cgroup is left on the machine (find /sys/fs/cgroup -name 'submeter-probe*' gives 0); every probe printed 'removed: True'.
